clue.text: One drinking like a fish? A shark, right

parts.note: the tope is a small shark found in British waters

explanation.surface: A heavy drinker is compared to a fish, then pinned down as a particular shark.
explanation.definitionFit: A toper is a habitual heavy drinker, someone who drinks hard like the proverbial fish.

clue.text: Could be a minute clock?

parts.note: a minute is a span of time, a piece of time, and a tiny clock could also be called a watch

explanation.surface: A question about whether a tiny clock is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: A timepiece is any clock or watch; a minute is also literally a portion of time.

clue.text: Found in Pennsylvania and put in a zoo

definitions.text: Found in Pennsylvania and put in a zoo

indicators.note: the word and is put in, placed inside, the state's abbreviation

parts.note: PA is the postal abbreviation for Pennsylvania

explanation.surface: An animal discovered in an American state is sent off to a zoo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put in' places AND inside PA, giving P-AND-A.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant panda is a bear famous as a zoo attraction.

clue.text: Hence a glimmering that the onset is easy to bear

parts.note: a rush is a sudden onset or charge
something light is not heavy, easy to carry

explanation.surface: A faint light is promised because the start of something is gentle.
explanation.definitionFit: A rushlight was a feeble candle of rush pith dipped in fat, giving a faint glimmer.

clue.text: See about strong language — to me it's disgusting

indicators.note: the word for see goes around the bad language, holding it inside

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see
oaths are swear words, strong language
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone finds swearing repellent and says so personally.
explanation.walkthrough: LO split open by OATHS gives LOATHSO; 'to me' adds ME at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Loathsome means hateful or repellent, a close synonym of disgusting.

clue.text: Inspection of King's Scholar on end of line in Cornish resort

indicators.note: the scholar and line's end sit inside the Cornish town's name

parts.note: Looe is a seaside town in Cornwall

indicators.note: in a down clue the scholar sits on top of the line's final letter

parts.note: KS stands for King's Scholar, a scholarship pupil at schools such as Eton

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A scholarship boy is inspected on a seaside holiday in Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: LOOE is opened after LOO to take KS plus E, the end of 'line'.
explanation.definitionFit: A look-see is an informal quick inspection, a glance over something.

clue.text: Article on Italian poet's movement

indicators.note: in a down clue the article is placed on top of the poet's name

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
Dante is the great Italian poet; the 's is no letter

explanation.surface: A piece of writing about an Italian poet's movements.
explanation.definitionFit: Andante is a musical tempo marking, and a movement of a symphony can carry that name.

clue.text: Pleonastically male ram gets us agitated

parts.note: he is used for a male animal, as he-goat
a tup is a ram

explanation.surface: A redundantly described male sheep upsets everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pleonastically' (redundantly) admits that HE-TUP says male twice, since a tup is already male; it adds no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Het up is an informal phrase for excited and anxious.

clue.text: Bowling strength so to defeat the opposition

parts.note: an over is a set of six balls bowled in cricket
power is strength

explanation.surface: A cricket team's strong bowling beats the other side.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an OVER is a set of six deliveries by one bowler.
explanation.definitionFit: To overpower is to overcome or subdue by superior force.

clue.text: Number three perhaps?

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the word three might be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: A query about whether three is one example of a number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' looks like a figure but means something that numbs, an anaesthetic.
explanation.definitionFit: Ether was an early anaesthetic, something that numbs a patient.

clue.text: One's in order having this cover for a poisonous plant

parts.note: a monk is one in a religious order; the 's makes it possessive
a hood is a head covering

explanation.surface: A member of a religious order wears a cowl that turns out to be a toxic flower.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant's name reads literally as a monk's cowl, which the clue describes as the cover such a person has.
explanation.definitionFit: Monkshood, also called aconite or wolfsbane, is a highly toxic garden flower.

clue.text: They bite a bit at times

definitions.text: They bite a bit at times

parts.words: They bite a bit at times
parts.note: a playful description of the things in the mouth that bite, and that a horse's bit sits behind

explanation.surface: Something nips occasionally, like a mildly bad-tempered dog.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the hard structures in the jaw used for biting food.

clue.text: Fruit many swine will not appreciate

parts.note: a pear is a fruit
L, the Roman numeral for fifty, stands for many in crosswords

explanation.surface: Pigs are said to turn their snouts up at a certain fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition alludes to the saying 'casting pearls before swine', offering something precious to those who cannot value it.
explanation.definitionFit: In the biblical proverb pigs cannot value gems from oysters thrown before them.

clue.text: Bird in the hand of a Cockney wood-worker, say?

indicators.text: in the hand of a Cockney
indicators.note: a Cockney speaker's vowels turn the woodworking tool's name into a different word when spoken

parts.note: sandpaper is an example of something that works wood smooth

explanation.surface: A bird held in the hand of a London carpenter.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cockney is a working-class Londoner; the accent says the 'ay' of paper like 'eye', so sandpaper comes out as the wading bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The sandpiper is a small wading shorebird.

clue.text: Limits of epic record said to be Virgil's work

indicators.note: the limits of a word are its first and last letters
spoken aloud, the record word gives the ending of the poem's name

parts.note: a log is a written record, as a ship's log

explanation.surface: Bits of an epic record are attributed to a Roman poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgil's Eclogues are a set of ten pastoral poems, each one a short pastoral dialogue.

clue.text: A queen's favourite cheese

explanation.surface: A monarch's best-loved cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, was a favourite courtier of Elizabeth I; Red Leicester is an English cheese.

clue.text: Do we finally get supplied with funds?

indicators.note: the word for finally gets, takes in, the two opening words

parts.note: the end comes finally
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether they will at last receive some money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get' tells END to take in DOWE, giving EN-DOWE-D.
explanation.definitionFit: To endow is to give a permanent income or fund, so an endowed body has been provided with money.

clue.text: One giving us medicines or one doing without?

explanation.surface: A pharmacist, or someone who manages without.
explanation.definitionFit: A pharmacist dispenses drugs; to dispense with something is to do without it.

clue.text: Hamlet a king of infinite space if so untroubled by visions?

definitions.text: Hamlet a king of infinite space if so untroubled by visions?

parts.words: Hamlet a king of infinite space if so untroubled by visions?
parts.note: Hamlet says he could be bounded in a nutshell and count himself a king of infinite space, were it not that he has bad dreams

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare quotation: Hamlet would rule infinite space if his sleep were untroubled.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleep free of nocturnal visions is the condition Hamlet wishes for.

clue.text: Could be Pauline writing this

parts.note: a description of a New Testament letter attributed to St Paul, disguised as a woman named Pauline writing

explanation.surface: A woman called Pauline might be the author of this text.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pauline books of the New Testament are letters from the apostle to churches.

clue.text: See unfinished music composition, Abode of the Blessed

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city, and a see is a bishop's diocese

indicators.note: composition means putting together, so the letters are arranged afresh
unfinished means the last letter is lost

explanation.surface: A bishop's seat, an incomplete piece of music, and heaven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' cuts MUSIC to MUSI, and 'composition' rearranges that as SIUM.
explanation.definitionFit: Elysium, the Elysian Fields, was the Greek paradise for heroes and the virtuous after death.

clue.text: Abide by notice

explanation.surface: An instruction to obey a sign posted up.
explanation.definitionFit: To observe a rule is to comply with it; to observe something is also to see or note it.

clue.text: Tragic hero to die terribly in work

indicators.note: the rearranged word sits inside the word for work

parts.note: opus is Latin for a work, used of musical compositions

indicators.note: terribly means the word die is mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: A tragic figure is doomed to perish horribly within a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' turns DIE into EDI, which goes inside OPUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Oedipus, of Sophocles' play, killed his father and married his mother unknowingly.

clue.text: Discerning the archaic style — exculpated about that

indicators.note: the word for exculpated goes around the old form, enclosing it

parts.note: to be exculpated is to be cleared of blame
ye is an archaic way of writing the

explanation.surface: A perceptive verdict on an old-fashioned style, acquitting it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts YE inside CLEARED, after CLEARE.
explanation.definitionFit: Clear-eyed means seeing things clearly and realistically, that is perceptive.

clue.text: Periodical appearance of variety entertainer

explanation.surface: A regular showing by a music-hall turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A comic is a children's illustrated magazine and also a stand-up comedian.

clue.text: William's sound advice to give us overhead cover

definitions.note: William II of England's nickname, the red

indicators.note: the instruction, spoken aloud, gives the king's epithet

parts.words: advice to give us overhead cover
parts.note: roof us is an urging to put a roof over us

explanation.surface: A king named William offers wise counsel about shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: William II of England was known as William RUFUS; 'sound advice' looks like good advice.
explanation.definitionFit: William II was nicknamed Rufus, Latin for red, for his ruddy complexion.

clue.text: Where for instance to get meat in Surrey

parts.note: e.g. is the abbreviation for for example, for instance
ham is cured pork, a meat

explanation.surface: A question about a place to buy meat in a county near London.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is a county just south-west of London; EGHAM is a town there, near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: Egham is a Surrey town, so it answers the question of which place.

clue.text: It makes one a hit in the West Indies

indicators.note: makes means the letters of a hit are made into something new

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Something proves a success in the Caribbean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' turns A HIT into HAIT; I for 'one' follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Haiti is a Caribbean country on the island of Hispaniola.

clue.text: The theme is witticism, a Kipling poem

parts.note: mot, short for bon mot, is a witty remark
If is a famous poem by Rudyard Kipling

explanation.surface: A literary point: the subject of Kipling's verse is wit.
explanation.definitionFit: A motif is a recurring idea or subject in a work, its leading idea.

clue.text: I am a voice without emotion

parts.note: I'm is the contraction of I am
passive is a grammatical voice, opposite to active

explanation.surface: A speaker describes their own flat, unfeeling tone of voice.
explanation.definitionFit: Impassive means showing no feeling, expressionless.

clue.text: Time for stocking up, you'll say?

definitions.text: Time for stocking up, you'll say?

parts.words: Time for stocking up, you'll say?
parts.note: stocking up sounds like laying in supplies but means the season when stockings are hung up for presents

explanation.surface: Someone suggests it is the season to lay in provisions.
explanation.definitionFit: Children hang up stockings on the eve of this December festival for gifts from Santa.

clue.text: Victims of Cromwell according to Marie

definitions.text: Victims of Cromwell according to Marie

parts.words: Victims of Cromwell according to Marie
parts.note: the music-hall singer Marie Lloyd sang of being one of these that Cromwell knocked about a bit

explanation.surface: A historical claim about Cromwell's victims credited to someone named Marie.
explanation.walkthrough: Marie Lloyd's British music-hall song 'One of the Ruins that Cromwell Knocked About a Bit'; Cromwell's troops wrecked many castles and abbeys in the Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: Cromwell's forces left castles and churches as wrecked remains.
